column1: Shell brace expansion: what does `pre{a,b,c}post` produce, and at what stage does it happen?
column2:
pre{a,b,c}post  ->  preapost prebpost precpost   (one copy per comma-separated item)

Happens FIRST — before variable expansion, before globbing, before the command runs.
Pure text: it never checks the filesystem (unlike a glob such as *).

Ranges:  {1..5} -> 1 2 3 4 5     {a..e} -> a b c d e
Preview safely with:  echo pre{a,b,c}post

column1: Shell: rename `config` to `config.bak` in one command without retyping the path?
column2:
mv config{,.bak}        ->  mv config config.bak

The empty item ("") gives the original name; ".bak" gives the backup. The shell
expands it before mv runs. Works BECAUSE it's text expansion, not globbing — the
.bak target doesn't exist yet, so a glob couldn't produce it.

Reverse:  mv config{.bak,}   ->  mv config.bak config

column1: Bash parameter expansion: what do `#`, `##`, `%`, `%%` strip, and how do you get a basename / drop an extension?
column2:
Strip a GLOB pattern from the value:
  #   shortest leading (prefix)      ##  longest leading
  %   shortest trailing (suffix)     %%  longest trailing
Mnemonic: # is LEFT of the number keys -> prefix; % is RIGHT -> suffix. Doubled = greedy.

path="/a/b/file.md"
  ${path##*/}  -> file.md    (basename — longest leading */)
  ${path%/*}   -> /a/b       (dirname  — shortest trailing /*)
f="a.tar.gz"
  ${f%.*}      -> a.tar      (drop last extension)
  ${f##*.}     -> gz         (extension only)

column1: tmux: why can't a single press of your prefix (e.g. Ctrl+a) also act as its normal key in the shell, and what's the workaround?
column2:
The prefix is always intercepted and held to see the next key — that's its job — so it
can never fall through to the pane's program.

Workarounds:
  - bind-key C-a send-prefix  -> double-tap sends ONE literal keystroke to the app
    (so prefix C-a can still reach readline's beginning-of-line).
  - Or choose a prefix you never need in-app (e.g. C-Space) and drop send-prefix.

Gotcha: a prefix the compositor grabs (Ctrl+Space = common layout/IME toggle) never
reaches tmux at all.

column1: tmux `new-session`: what do `-s`, `-A`, `-d`, `-c` do, and how do they stack?
column2:
-s NAME   session name
-A        attach if NAME exists, else create (idempotent)
-d        detached — create but DON'T attach the current client
-c DIR    starting directory

Stack them:  -As NAME (attach-or-create)   -ds NAME (create detached)

column1: tmux: already inside tmux, you want to jump to session X (create if needed). Why not `new-session -A`, and what do you use instead?
column2:
new-session -A would ATTACH -> a session nested inside a session (tmux warns, confusing).

Inside tmux, create-detached then switch:
  tmux new-session -ds X 2>/dev/null   # make it if absent; ignore "exists"
  tmux switch-client -t X              # move THIS client — no nesting
Existence guard if you prefer:  tmux has-session -t X

column1: tmux: why is `.` illegal in a session name, and how do you sanitize a directory name into one?
column2:
Target syntax is  session:window.pane , so '.' is the window.pane separator — illegal
in a name.

Sanitize:  name="${name//./-}"   (or:  tr . -)
That's why tmux-sessionizer does  basename ... | tr . - .

column1: Shape of a `ts` helper: jump to a named tmux session, create on demand, safe inside AND outside tmux?
column2:
name="${1:-${PWD##*/}}"     # arg, else current dir basename
name="${name//./-}"         # '.' illegal in session names
if [[ -n "$TMUX" ]]; then   # inside tmux
  tmux new-session -ds "$name" 2>/dev/null
  tmux switch-client -t "$name"     # no nesting
else
  tmux new-session -As "$name"      # attach-or-create
fi

Key decision: the $TMUX branch — inside tmux, attaching would nest, so detach-create + switch.
